methodology.text:
A Synthetic Multi-Modal Patient Profile for Stage 3 Chronic Kidney Disease: Clinical and Wearable Data Integration
Subject: Azalee124 Raymonde315 Maggio310 (synthetic)
1. Clinical Data Generation
1.1 Population synthesis
A synthetic patient population (n=1,774, Massachusetts) was generated using Synthea, an open-source clinical simulation engine that models disease progression, care encounters, and treatment through condition-specific state machines calibrated against US epidemiological data.
1.2 Candidate identification
CKD Stage 3 candidates were initially identified by SNOMED code lookup (431857002). Manual verification of matched records revealed inconsistent code-to-display-text mappings within this Synthea build — the same code appeared attached to both Stage 3 and Stage 4 display labels across different patients, and the eventual study subject’s own “Stage 3” condition carried a code (433144002) conventionally associated with Stage 5. Code-based identification was therefore judged unreliable for this dataset.
Inspection of Synthea’s underlying CKD module (chronic_kidney_disease.json) confirmed that disease progression is governed by an internal severity attribute rather than a fixed code table, with staging text generated downstream of the core simulation logic — explaining the observed code/label drift.
Candidate selection was consequently redefined on clinical criteria rather than diagnostic codes: most recent estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR, MDRD formula) between 30–59 mL/min/1.73m², with exclusion of any patient record indicating dialysis, transplant, or end-stage renal disease. This yielded 69 candidates meeting Stage 3 criteria.
1.3 Subject selection and validation
The study subject was selected from this pool on the basis of eGFR value (45.4 mL/min/1.73m², mid-range Stage 3) and longitudinal data depth (95 recorded GFR measurements). Selection was confirmed against four independent criteria:
An explicit Condition-level diagnostic label (“Chronic kidney disease stage 3 (disorder)”), onset 2020-03-12, independent of the eGFR-based inclusion criterion
A clinically coherent progression sequence — Stage 1 (2011-06) → Stage 2 (2011-12) → Stage 3 (2020-03) — with no further progression to Stage 4/5 through the most recent record (2026), and no dialysis or transplant history
A comorbidity profile consistent with the diabetic-nephropathy pathway: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, essential hypertension, ischemic heart disease, obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, anemia, and metabolic syndrome
An active medication regimen consistent with the above comorbidities (beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor/calcium channel blocker/diuretic combination, insulin and metformin, inhaled bronchodilator/corticosteroid)
2. Wearable Data Source Selection
2.1 Target demographic profile
Female, date of birth 1940-07-25 (age 86 at time of most recent clinical record), White.
2.2 Donor pool constraints
Wearable baseline data were drawn from LifeSnaps, a longitudinal multimodal dataset (n=71 participants, Fitbit Sense, four-month collection period). LifeSnaps records participant gender and a binary age indicator (<30 / ≥30) but no exact age and no race or ethnicity field. Consequently:
Race could not be matched — the attribute is absent from the source dataset
Age matching was constrained to a single binary threshold, which all adult participants satisfy equally regardless of exact age
Gender was matched directly
2.3 Selection procedure
Filtering to female participants aged ≥30 yielded 12 candidates, demographically indistinguishable beyond this point given dataset constraints. Selection among these candidates used physiological indicators associated with cardiometabolic risk — resting heart rate and daily step count — as a proxy for consistency with the diabetic/hypertensive pathway underlying the subject’s CKD etiology. The selected participant exhibited the highest resting heart rate (72.9 bpm) and lowest mean daily step count (5,610) among candidates with complete heart rate variability (RMSSD) data, yielding 110 days of daily- and hourly-resolution Fitbit data.
3. Physiological Modification for Stage 3 CKD
3.1 Severity calibration
Modifications were calibrated to represent a stable Stage 3a CKD physiological profile rather than a progressive decline, consistent with the subject’s documented six-year plateau at Stage 3 (2020–2026) without progression to Stage 4/5.
3.2 Comorbidity-adjusted parameterization
Modification magnitudes were adjusted for the subject’s specific pharmacological and comorbid context rather than applied as generic CKD signatures:
Chronic beta-blocker therapy (metoprolol succinate) attenuates the expected resting heart rate elevation associated with CKD-related volume overload
Comorbid obstructive sleep apnea was modeled as an additive source of nocturnal oxygen desaturation, layered on baseline CKD-related hypoxemia risk
Comorbid anemia and ischemic heart disease were treated as compounding factors for reduced exercise tolerance and heart rate variability suppression, respectively

3.4 Application method
Modifications were applied as independent stochastic perturbations to each recorded (non-missing) value, preserving the direction of effect per parameter while allowing day-to-day magnitude to vary — retaining the natural variability structure of the source data rather than imposing a uniform shift. Missing values in the source data were preserved as missing; no values were imputed for sensor gaps in the original recording.
Acute exacerbation events were not modeled. All modifications represent a single stable disease-severity state; no simulated infection, decompensation, or hospitalization-level event is present in the dataset. The single exception is the nightly oxygen desaturation mechanism (Section 3.3), which represents the pre-existing sleep apnea diagnosis rather than a renal exacerbation.
4. Temporal Alignment
The wearable dataset’s native collection window (2021-10-05 to 2022-01-22) preceded the clinical record’s most recent entries by approximately five years. To represent a current physiological snapshot consistent with the subject’s present-day clinical status, the wearable time series was shifted forward by a constant offset such that the window terminates at the present date (2026-05-19 to 2026-09-05), preserving all relative day-to-day structure. The nearest clinical eGFR measurement to this window (45.4 mL/min/1.73m², recorded 2026-07-09) falls within the same Stage 3a classification used for severity calibration.
5. Data Files

modified_hourly.csv — hourly-resolution wearable data, 110 days

limitations.text:
Limitations — CKD Stage 3 Synthetic Patient Profile
Clinical Data (Synthea)
Vital signs disconnected from disease state: HbA1c and BMI identical across every reading despite active diabetes diagnosis
Blood pressure values normotensive despite hypertension diagnosis and 3-drug antihypertensive regimen
eGFR fluctuates independently of the serum creatinine value it is calculated from
Some conditions (e.g., prediabetes) remain “active” after being clinically superseded
Single simulated life path — no alternative disease trajectories represented
Wearable Donor Selection (LifeSnaps)
Race not matchable — attribute absent from source dataset
Age matchable only at a coarse threshold (<30 / ≥30), not exact age
Donor pool likely skews younger/healthier than a real CKD population
Selection heuristic (resting HR + step count as risk proxy) is reasoned, not empirically validated
Unmeasured confounders in the donor’s original recording period inherited without detection
Physiological Modification
Modification magnitudes are literature-informed estimates, not fitted to validated wearable-CKD outcome data
Parameters modified independently per field; limited cross-correlation between related metrics
No day-to-day inertia — real chronic illness trajectories are not this uniform
No acute exacerbation modeling — represents a stable state only
Confirmed inconsistency: daily vs. hourly step totals diverge 10–40% on most days
Data Integration
Clinical–wearable correspondence is constructed (sex-matched, risk-proxy-ranked), not a unified measurement process
No downstream validation against clinical judgment or an established wearable-based CKD detection method
